claims.text: Adding 0.5–1.0 wt% yttrium to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance.
Adding 0.5–1.0 wt% yttrium will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity under fusion-reactor conditions.
The baseline RHEA has a predominantly single-phase structure.
Yttrium addition promotes formation of stable yttrium-rich nanoprecipitates, including yttrium oxides.
The yttrium-rich nanoprecipitates form both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The yttrium-rich nanoprecipitates act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects and defect clusters.
The nanoprecipitates capture and immobilize irradiation-induced defects.
Capture of irradiation-induced defects by the nanoprecipitates reduces void formation and radiation damage.
Under high-temperature irradiation, mobile vacancies can agglomerate into voids or vacancy-type loops, while interstitial defects can agglomerate into dislocation loops.
A nanoscale dispersion of secondary particles reinforces grain boundaries and maintains or improves hardness.
The yttrium-modified RHEA will have significantly fewer irradiation-induced defects, voids, and dislocation loops than the unmodified alloy.
The yttrium-modified RHEA will maintain or improve nanoindentation hardness after irradiation relative to the unmodified alloy.
A large irradiation-induced hardness increase can indicate undesirable embrittlement.
The unmodified baseline RHEA accumulates measurable irradiation defects and may undergo void swelling.
The proposed benefit holds specifically within the 0.5–1.0 wt% yttrium range.
The proposed benefit holds under fusion-relevant high-temperature and high-flux irradiation.
Higher yttrium concentrations, different irradiation regimes, or excessive oxidation may negate the benefit.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant defect reduction, or observation of mechanical degradation relative to the baseline, would falsify the hypothesis.
